title: From DNA Route to Gene Order

scenes.tts: A bacterium gained a useful gene. What carried it there, and can that journey reveal a map? Watch the donor DNA, shown in gold. Bacteria do not make meiotic crosses, yet donor genes can become inherited.
scenes.caption: A bacterium gained a useful gene. What carried it there, and can that journey reveal a map? Watch the donor DNA, shown in gold. Bacteria do not make meiotic crosses, yet donor genes can become inherited.
scenes.visual: Build one continuous 16:9 schematic world. COLOUR MAP used throughout both films: donor DNA GOLD; recipient bacterium LIGHT GREY; donor bacterium TEAL; phage PURPLE; F factor ORANGE; recipient chromosome WHITE; filter BLUE; DNase RED. A large grey recipient fills the right half. Three question-mark paths approach from the left. A gold DNA segment travels along each path while faint particles drift. Keep a small 'schematic' label at bottom right. On the question, the three paths brighten without revealing their carriers.
scenes.narration: A bacterium gained a useful gene. What carried it there, and can that journey reveal a map? Watch the donor DNA, shown in gold. Bacteria do not make meiotic crosses, yet donor genes can become inherited.

scenes.visual: Title 'From DNA Route to Gene Order' appears above the same recipient for two seconds. Gold DNA continues moving slowly along the three unknown paths.

scenes.tts: One path exposes free DNA for transformation. Another joins donor and recipient for conjugation. The third protects donor DNA inside a phage during transduction. Competent cells take up the free DNA.
scenes.caption: One path exposes free DNA for transformation. Another joins donor and recipient for conjugation. The third protects donor DNA inside a phage during transduction. Competent cells take up the free DNA.
scenes.visual: Reveal the three carriers by transforming the question marks in place. Top: a bare GOLD fragment drifts toward the recipient, labelled 'transformation'. Middle: a TEAL donor touches the grey recipient and passes gold DNA, labelled 'conjugation'. Bottom: a PURPLE phage carries a gold block, labelled 'transduction'. Keep the recipient fixed while each path moves.
scenes.narration: One path exposes free DNA for transformation. Another joins donor and recipient for conjugation. The third protects donor DNA inside a phage during transduction. Competent cells take up the free DNA.

scenes.tts: A filter that stops cells blocks only the contact path. Deoxyribonuclease destroys exposed DNA, but a phage coat protects its cargo. That two-step test turns three pictures into a decision.
scenes.caption: A filter that stops cells blocks only the contact path. DNase destroys exposed DNA, but a phage coat protects its cargo. That two-step test turns three pictures into a decision.
scenes.visual: A tall BLUE filter slides between carriers and recipient. The teal donor stops, while the bare fragment and purple phage pass through pores. Then a RED sweep labelled 'DNase' dissolves the bare gold fragment. The gold block inside the purple phage remains visible and moving.
scenes.narration: A filter that stops cells blocks only the contact path. DNase destroys exposed DNA, but a phage coat protects its cargo. That two-step test turns three pictures into a decision.

scenes.tts: An unknown transfer survives the enzyme, but stops when cells are separated. Which carrier fits? Follow both clues before choosing. One result rules out free DNA. The other rules out a phage.
scenes.caption: An unknown transfer survives the enzyme, but stops when cells are separated. Which carrier fits? Follow both clues before choosing. One result rules out free DNA. The other rules out a phage.
scenes.visual: Reset all three paths to neutral outlines. Show two large evidence cards: 'survives DNase' with an intact gold block, and 'stops at filter' with a blocked path. Place transformation, conjugation and transduction icons beneath them. The question 'Which carrier fits both clues?' fills the upper third.
scenes.narration: An unknown transfer survives the enzyme, but stops when cells are separated. Which carrier fits? Follow both clues before choosing. One result rules out free DNA. The other rules out a phage.

scenes.visual: Deliberate predict pause. Hold the evidence cards and three carrier icons. The gold blocks bob gently and the filter shimmers; reveal nothing.

scenes.tts: Conjugation fits. Its DNA is never exposed, so the enzyme misses it. Separating the cells removes the connection it needs. Both clues point to direct contact, not merely DNA moving through the medium.
scenes.caption: Conjugation fits. Its DNA is never exposed, so the enzyme misses it. Separating the cells removes the connection it needs. Both clues point to direct contact, not merely DNA moving through the medium.
scenes.visual: The transformation and phage icons dim without rejection marks. The TEAL donor and grey recipient enlarge and make contact. Gold DNA crosses their connection. The red DNase sweep passes outside harmlessly. The blue filter then slides between them and the connection retracts.
scenes.narration: Conjugation fits. Its DNA is never exposed, so the enzyme misses it. Separating the cells removes the connection it needs. Both clues point to direct contact, not merely DNA moving through the medium.

scenes.tts: In E coli, the F factor is a small DNA circle. Free F transfers itself from a donor to a recipient. One strand crosses from F plus to F minus, and each cell completes the circle. Chromosomal markers rarely follow.
scenes.caption: In E. coli, the F factor is a small DNA circle. Free F transfers itself from a donor to a recipient. One strand crosses from F+ to F−, and each cell completes the circle. Chromosomal markers rarely follow.
scenes.visual: Keep the same cell pair. An ORANGE circle labelled 'F' appears inside the teal donor. One orange strand unrolls through the connection, then each cell completes an orange circle. Labels change from 'F+' and 'F−' to 'F+' on both cells. The WHITE chromosome stays still.
scenes.narration: In E. coli, the F factor is a small DNA circle. Free F transfers itself from a donor to a recipient. One strand crosses from F+ to F−, and each cell completes the circle. Chromosomal markers rarely follow.

scenes.tts: When F joins the donor chromosome, the cell is H F R. Transfer now pulls chromosomal markers through the same origin in a fixed order. Because pairs usually separate early, recipients receive only part of the chromosome. The remaining F sequence would arrive last.
scenes.caption: When F joins the donor chromosome, the cell is Hfr. Transfer now pulls chromosomal markers through the same origin in a fixed order. Because pairs usually separate early, recipients receive only part of the chromosome. The remaining F sequence would arrive last.
scenes.visual: Transform the orange F circle into one orange segment embedded in the donor's large WHITE chromosome ring. Label the donor 'Hfr'. Open the ring at the orange origin into a long moving strip. GOLD marker blocks on the strip pass through the connection one after another while a fixed arrow shows transfer direction.
scenes.narration: When F joins the donor chromosome, the cell is Hfr. Transfer now pulls chromosomal markers through the same origin in a fixed order. Because pairs usually separate early, recipients receive only part of the chromosome. The remaining F sequence would arrive last.

scenes.tts: Break different pairs apart at different times, then score the recipients. Markers nearer the origin appear first. With steady transfer, the time gaps become map distances. Selective plates reveal which recipients inherited each marker. A marker's entry time is the earliest interruption that still yields it.
scenes.caption: Break different pairs apart at different times, then score the recipients. Markers nearer the origin appear first. With steady transfer, the time gaps become map distances. Selective plates reveal which recipients inherited each marker. A marker's entry time is the earliest interruption that still yields it.
scenes.visual: Duplicate the moving pair into four rows without shrinking the main action below sixty percent of frame height overall. A sweeping interruption bar stops each row later. Gold markers already across settle onto one shared horizontal timeline. Marker order becomes a gene map; labelled brackets between markers grow from the time gaps. Show no numbers.
scenes.narration: Break different pairs apart at different times, then score the recipients. Markers nearer the origin appear first. With steady transfer, the time gaps become map distances. Selective plates reveal which recipients inherited each marker. A marker's entry time is the earliest interruption that still yields it.

scenes.tts: A different H F R origin can send the same chromosome the other way. Absolute arrival times change, but matching gaps reveal one circular map. The origin sets the starting time, so absolute times cannot be compared directly across donors.
scenes.caption: A different Hfr origin can send the same chromosome the other way. Absolute arrival times change, but matching gaps reveal one circular map. The origin sets the starting time, so absolute times cannot be compared directly across donors.
scenes.visual: Bend the linear map back into a large WHITE chromosome circle. Move the ORANGE origin to the opposite side and reverse its arrow. The same gold markers leave in reverse order. Their interval brackets detach, rotate, and align exactly with the first set before both maps close into one circle.
scenes.narration: A different Hfr origin can send the same chromosome the other way. Absolute arrival times change, but matching gaps reveal one circular map. The origin sets the starting time, so absolute times cannot be compared directly across donors.

scenes.tts: Selection makes rare recipients visible, but a colony reports more than arrival. The donor piece must also be expressed and usually integrated. Incoming linear DNA cannot copy itself with the chromosome. Recombination can replace the matching recipient segment.
scenes.caption: Selection makes rare recipients visible, but a colony reports more than arrival. The donor piece must also be expressed and usually integrated. Incoming linear DNA cannot copy itself with the chromosome. Recombination can replace the matching recipient segment.
scenes.visual: The chromosome circle shrinks into one grey recipient on a large plate. Most cells fade; a few colonies expand. Above one colony, animate three linked tokens in order: 'entry', 'integration', 'expression'. Keep each token visible as the next appears, with gold DNA joining the white recipient chromosome at the integration step.
scenes.narration: Selection makes rare recipients visible, but a colony reports more than arrival. The donor piece must also be expressed and usually integrated. Incoming linear DNA cannot copy itself with the chromosome. Recombination can replace the matching recipient segment.

scenes.tts: The route created the readout. For H F R transfer, ordered arrival maps gene order. If transfer is roughly steady, time gaps also map distance. Keep the gaps, not the clock's starting values.
scenes.caption: The route created the readout. For Hfr transfer, ordered arrival maps gene order. If transfer is roughly steady, time gaps also map distance. Keep the gaps, not the clock's starting values.
scenes.visual: Return to the large teal donor and grey recipient. Their moving gold chromosome strip transforms into the marker timeline and then the gene map. Hold the map while the interval brackets pulse once.
scenes.narration: The route created the readout. For Hfr transfer, ordered arrival maps gene order. If transfer is roughly steady, time gaps also map distance. Keep the gaps, not the clock's starting values.

scenes.visual: End card over the dimmed moving timeline. Show one centred line only: 'Ordered arrival maps gene order; time gaps map distance.' Gold markers continue drifting slowly behind it.
